title: Retinal center-surround sense amp referencing six averaged neighbour bitlines
idea: Like retinal horizontal cells that subtract the local mean, each sense amp compares its bitline against the capacitively averaged voltage of six unselected bitlines in the adjacent mat (a passive BEOL coupling-cap network switched in during sensing), so wordline coupling, plate bounce and substrate noise cancel as common mode. Averaging six references cuts reference noise by about 2.4x versus one.
why: Fact 1 capacitor wall: common-mode noise and reference mismatch eat ~30-40% of sense margin; cancelling it could let Cs drop from ~5 fF to ~3 fF, so capacitor AR falls from 60-75:1 to ~40:1 with fewer etch/deposition steps.

title: Hair-cell stochastic resonance: dithered mini-latch with majority vote
idea: Cochlear hair cells use stochastic resonance, where added noise helps a threshold detector see sub-threshold input. An isolated mini-comparator hanging off the bitline pair gets a controlled zero-mean dither on its tail node and fires 3-5 times in ~4 ns. A majority vote sets the main latch, which then restores the cell.
why: Fact 1/7: tolerates ~40% smaller bitline swing (60 mV vs 100 mV), so bitlines can carry 1024 cells instead of 512. That halves the sense-amp count and its stripe area, roughly 5-8% of the die, or allows smaller Cs.

title: Axon-hillock NbO2 spiking threshold element replacing large matched sense pairs
idea: Like the axon hillock's all-or-nothing spike, a nanoscale NbO2 Mott threshold switch plus series capacitor at each bitline pair forms a relaxation 'neuron'. It fires only when the differential charge passes a programmable bias threshold, turning a few-mV signal into a large spike that sets a minimal latch. Threshold is trimmed by bias, not by big matched transistors.
why: Fact 7: sense-amp input pairs are sized large to beat Vt mismatch. A trimmed spiking element could shrink sense-amp transistor area 3-4x and the sense-amp stripe ~25%.

title: Dendritic-tree row decoders in BEOL oxide transistors over the mats
idea: Dendrites compute at branch points, so build the row predecode/decode as a binary tree of 2-input coincidence (AND) gates made from IGZO or poly-Si TFTs in the BEOL directly above the cell mats. Pipelining hides TFT slowness. Only the final high-voltage wordline drivers stay in the silicon strip.
why: Fact 7: decoder strips are ~10-15% of the die. Moving the logic part into otherwise empty BEOL volume could shrink the die ~8-12% without hybrid-bonding capex.

title: Integrate-and-fire latency-code sensing with one shared comparator per 16 bitlines
idea: Like a neuron's latency code, each bitline discharges into a 2-transistor integrate-and-fire node whose firing time encodes stored charge, and 16 bitlines share one arbitrated time-to-digital comparator. A one-transistor restore pull per bitline is driven from the decoded result.
why: Fact 7: replaces a ~10-transistor cross-coupled sense amp per pair with ~3 small devices plus a shared TDC. Sense-amp area falls ~50-60%, about 8-10% of the die.

title: Photoreceptor light adaptation: reference voltage tracking time since refresh
idea: Like a photoreceptor shifting its operating point with ambient light, a per-bank reference generator walks the sense reference down the expected charge-loss curve since that row group's last refresh. A drooped '1' is then still compared against a threshold midway between the decayed '1' and the '0'.
why: Fact 3: a fixed mid-rail reference fails a '1' at VDD/2. A tracking reference roughly doubles the allowable droop, extending tREFW 1.5-2.5x and cutting refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) and the 10-20% bandwidth tax in proportion.

title: Electric-fish lock-in sensing via carrier-modulated cell plate and chopper demodulation
idea: Weakly electric fish detect nanovolt fields by emitting a carrier and demodulating synchronously. During the read window the bitline precharge reference carries a small GHz carrier, and a chopper switch pair at the sense-amp input demodulates it, moving the signal away from 1/f noise and slow offset drift before the latch fires.
why: Fact 1/10: removing offset and low-frequency noise (~30-40 mV equivalent) gives ~1.5-2x effective SNR. That buys ~40% smaller Cs, or VARY below 1 V for lower CV^2 energy.

title: Cochlear tonotopic row selection with frequency-addressed wordline groups
idea: Like the basilar membrane, where each position resonates at its own frequency, each local wordline-driver group gets a tiny on-die resonator (BAW/MEMS or LC) tuned to a unique frequency. The bank broadcasts one tone burst on a single shared line, and only the matching group rectifies it into a wordline enable, replacing predecode buses and one decoder level.
why: Fact 7: collapsing 64-way selection onto one wire could cut that decode level's area 30-50% and remove predecode bus switching energy.

title: Synaptic-vesicle charge packets shifted by bucket brigade to edge amplifiers
idea: Instead of a sense amp on every bitline pair, the activated row's charges move as discrete packets (like vesicles to a release site) through CCD-style transfer gates under each bitline. They reach a few high-quality correlated amplifiers at the mat edge, which digitize and write back by reverse transfer.
why: Fact 7: one amplifier per ~32 bitlines cuts sense-amp stripe area ~70% (~12-15% of the die). Random latency gets worse, so it suits streaming/AI-weight memory tiers.

title: Gap-junction wordline charge sharing between closing and opening rows
idea: Neurons joined by gap junctions pass charge directly. When one subarray's wordline (at VPP ~3 V) closes and another's opens, a pass switch first shorts the two, so about half the charge moves from the falling line to the rising one. The VPP pump then supplies only the remainder.
why: Fact 10: VPP comes from a ~30-40% efficient pump. Recycling ~50% of wordline charge cuts VPP energy ~40% and lets the pump, a large periphery block, shrink ~30%.

title: Chromatophore test pixels: optical wafer-wide readout of BIST results
idea: Cephalopod chromatophores show internal state on the skin. Each mat gets a tiny electrochromic (WO3/PEDOT) pad driven by its built-in self-test pass/fail latch. With power supplied through a few probe needles, a camera images the whole wafer during the BIST run and reads millions of mat results in parallel.
why: Testers cost millions and run for hours per wafer. Parallel optical readout could cut wafer-test time ~10x and shrink BIST/DFT I/O periphery, worth ~3-5% of cost per bit.

title: Magnetosome-chain anisotropic interconnect joining periphery wafer to array wafer
idea: Magnetotactic bacteria align magnetite crystals into chains. Fill a bonding dielectric with Fe3O4/Ni nanoparticles and cure it under a vertical magnetic field, so conductive pillar chains self-assemble at ~300 nm pitch. They join a separately made logic-process periphery wafer to the array wafer without fine-alignment hybrid bonding.
why: Fact 7 + capital: puts ~40% of periphery on a cheaper logic wafer under/over the array. Field-assembled ACF needs far less capex than hybrid-bond tools, and the die shrinks ~20-30%.

title: Venus-flytrap analog leaky integrators as row-hammer counters
idea: The Venus flytrap counts touches with a decaying calcium signal (two within ~30 s closes the trap). Each 8-row group gets a DRAM-process capacitor that takes a fixed charge packet per activation and leaks with a designed time constant near the refresh window. Crossing a comparator threshold triggers neighbor refresh, with no SRAM counters or CAM.
why: Fact 9: digital per-row counters cost ~1-2% of die and energy. An analog leaky counter is ~3 transistors plus one cell-type cap per group (~10x smaller) and forgets old activity by itself.

title: Kinetic-proofreading two-threshold sensing that heals marginal cells on access
idea: DNA polymerase rejects errors with an energy-spending delay (kinetic proofreading). The sense path samples each bitline against +delta then -delta references. Cells that resolve consistently restore normally. Cells inside the delta band get a boosted-VPP extended restore, and their address goes to a small weak-row table for faster refresh.
why: Fact 3: catches decaying cells during normal traffic before they fail, so baseline refresh can relax ~2x and refresh energy/bandwidth roughly halves.

title: Octopus-arm self-timed mats with replica-bitline handshakes
idea: Octopus arms run local reflex loops with little central control. Each mat generates its own sense-enable, restore-done and precharge-done events from replica bitlines (bundled-data asynchronous handshake). The bank logic sends only 'go' and receives 'done', with no worst-case global timing chains.
why: Typical mats finish 20-30% before worst-case tRCD/tRP. Self-timing raises bandwidth and cuts latency, and removes timing-generator wiring and margin (~10% of periphery power).

title: Olfactory combinatorial 3-of-24 constant-weight wordline decoder
idea: About 400 olfactory receptor types encode trillions of odors combinatorially. Replace one-hot predecode with a constant-weight code: each local wordline driver connects to a unique triplet of 24 shared select lines (2,024 triplets) through a vertical 3-gate stacked transistor. Only the triplet with all three lines high fires, and every other triplet has at most two high.
why: Fact 7: about 2-3x fewer predecode lines and decoder transistors than tree decoders, so row-decode area falls ~30%.

title: Electric-eel stacked charge pump built from spare array capacitors
idea: Electric eels stack thousands of electrocytes in series to reach 600 V. Build the VPP/VBB pumps from blocks of ordinary high-AR cell capacitors (dummy rows at mat edges, thousands in parallel), switched by array transistors into a series-parallel ladder stack, instead of planar MOS capacitors in the periphery.
why: Fact 7/10: pillar caps give ~50-100x more capacitance per area than planar caps. Pumps shrink ~5x (2-4% of die), and bigger flying caps raise pump efficiency ~1.5x.

title: Firefly anti-phase coupled oscillators that self-spread refresh bursts
idea: Pulse-coupled fireflies with inhibitory coupling settle into anti-phase. Each bank's local refresh oscillator senses neighbors' refresh current on a shared line and delays itself when they fire, so refresh bursts spread evenly in time across banks with no central scheduler.
why: Peak refresh current sets power-grid metal, decap area and IR-drop margin. Spreading cuts peak current 4-8x, letting grid and decaps shrink (~2-3% of die).

title: Dendritic-spine IGZO gain stage every 32 cells on short bitlines
idea: Dendritic spines amplify input in a tiny isolated compartment. A BEOL oxide-semiconductor 'spine' transistor every 32 cells takes the cell's charge from a very short local bitline (~1/16 the capacitance) and drives current onto the global bitline. A separate transfer gate writes back.
why: Fact 1/2: the Cs/Cbl transfer ratio improves ~10x, so Cs can fall from ~5 fF to ~1 fF with AR ~15:1 capacitors. That breaks the capacitor wall and makes 3D tiers practical.

title: Barn-owl Jeffress delay-line coincidence decoder on one wire pair
idea: Barn owls localize sound with counter-propagating axonal delay lines and coincidence-detector neurons. Pulses launch from both ends of a tapped delay-chain select wire, with their relative launch time encoding the row address. Only the driver where they meet sees both pulses inside its coincidence window and fires.
why: Fact 7: one wire pair plus a programmable launch delay replaces a multi-level decoder tree and predecode buses for 64-256 drivers, cutting decode area ~40% and decode energy.

title: Pacinian-corpuscle auto-zero sense amp responding only to change
idea: Pacinian corpuscles ignore steady pressure and respond only to change. Before the wordline fires, each sense amp stores its own input offset on small capacitors while the bitlines are equalized (auto-zero). It then senses only the change, cancelling latch Vt mismatch.
why: Fact 1/7: input devices are oversized to hold offset below ~10 mV. Offset cancellation lets them shrink ~4x, cutting sense-amp stripe area ~30% or Cs ~30%.

title: Ormia coupled-ear switched-capacitor lever doubling bitline differential
idea: The fly Ormia ochracea links its eardrums with a lever that magnifies tiny interaural differences. Before latching, two small caps sample the bitline differential in parallel and are then switched into series, a charge-pump 'lever' that doubles delta-V while common mode stays put. The doubled signal goes to a standard latch.
why: Fact 1/7: a 2x larger delta-V relaxes Cs/Cbl by 2x, giving Cs ~2.5 fF or double-length bitlines with half the sense amps.

title: Honeycomb mat tiling sharing each sense-amp hub among three mats
idea: Bees' hexagonal comb shares every wall between neighbors. Mats are tiled hexagonally so each sense-amp hub sits where three mats meet and is time-multiplexed among their bitlines: one active, one as open-bitline reference, one idle. Conventional open bitline shares between only two.
why: Fact 7: sense amps per bit fall ~1/3, so the sense-amp stripe shrinks ~30% and the die ~5-7%. The cell array is already hex-packed, so lithography fits.

title: Clonal-selection retention profiler RTL for commodity DDR5 on FPGA
idea: Like adaptive immunity, an FPGA controller (DRAM Bender-class) 'challenges' rows with stretched refresh and worst-case patterns. Failing rows are clonally expanded into a Bloom-filter list kept at 64 ms, and negative selection re-tests them to purge false positives and catch VRT drift. Everything else refreshes at 256 ms. Three engineers for 24 months plus $80k of boards, ~$900k total, produce licensable controller RTL.
why: Fact 3: ~4x fewer refreshes for >99.9% of rows saves ~70% of refresh energy and most of the 10-20% bandwidth tax, with no DRAM die change.

title: Chemotaxis run-and-tumble firmware harvesting per-bank timing guardband
idea: E. coli keeps running while conditions improve and tumbles when they worsen. Controller firmware nudges a bank's tRCD/tRP/tRAS down one clock at random and keeps the change while ECC scrubs and canary rows stay clean (run). It reverts and re-randomizes on any corrected error (tumble), tracking temperature and aging. About $500k of firmware and FPGA validation over 18 months.
why: Commodity timings carry 20-40% guardband. Harvesting ~20% lower latency adaptively raises useful bandwidth per DIMM, so fewer DIMMs serve a workload.

title: Synaptic-scaling refresh loop holding corrected errors at a set point
idea: Neurons scale synapses to keep firing near a homeostatic set point. A controller loop stretches each rank's refresh interval additively until host/on-die ECC corrected-error counts reach a tiny target (e.g., 1 per 10^14 bit-hours). It shrinks the interval multiplicatively on any rise and snaps to the JEDEC rate when errors cluster. Firmware plus a 12-month soak on 200 DIMMs, ~$700k.
why: Fact 3: cool datacenter DIMMs could safely run 2-3x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy/bandwidth ~50% with zero hardware change.

title: Murray's-law tapered power-tree generator for DRAM periphery
idea: Blood vessels and leaf veins follow Murray's law (parent radius^3 = sum of children's), minimizing transport cost per volume. An open-source EDA plugin synthesizes periphery VDD/VPP/VSS distribution as Murray-tapered trees instead of uniform meshes, with IR-drop sign-off on a test layout. Two engineers plus licenses, ~$600k in 24 months, then licensed to DRAM/eDRAM teams.
why: Fact 7 + tungsten chokepoint: ~20-30% less periphery power metal at equal IR drop frees routing tracks and cuts W/Cu usage in the lower levels.

title: Physarum flux-reinforcement floorplanner for global data and command buses
idea: The slime mould Physarum thickens tubes that carry flow and prunes the rest, finding near-optimal networks. Its flux-reinforcement model drives the routing of a DRAM die's global data, command and test buses, weighted by real access traces. Software only, ~$400k over 18 months, released and licensed.
why: Fact 5/7: trace-weighted Physarum topologies can cut weighted global wirelength ~10-20%, with similar savings in internal data-movement energy and bus area.

title: Ant-colony optimizer for spare row and column repair allocation
idea: Ants find short paths with depositing and evaporating pheromone. Ant-colony optimization solves the NP-hard redundancy-allocation problem (which spares fix a fail bitmap) on tester-side GPUs, approaching optimal repair. Two engineers plus partner fail bitmaps, ~$500k in 24 months.
why: Fact 7: spares, fuses and compare logic are several % of the die. Equal repair with ~25% fewer spares, or +1-3% repair yield on today's spares, cuts cost/bit directly.

title: Genetic-programming evolved sense-amp netlists proven on SkyWater 130 shuttle
idea: Sense-amp netlists are treated as genomes and evolved by mutation and recombination in open-source SPICE on cloud CPUs, selecting for Monte-Carlo offset, area and energy. The top 10 survivors tape out on an open SkyWater 130 shuttle next to a classic latch. Compute $100k plus shuttle/test $150k plus 2 engineers, ~$750k in 24 months.
why: Fact 1/7: may find sense amps with ~30% less area or 2x lower offset per area, licensable to DRAM makers.

title: Hopf-critical oscillator sense amp poised at edge of oscillation
idea: Cochlear outer hair cells sit near a Hopf bifurcation for huge gain on faint sound. A tiny oscillator is biased just below onset, so a few-mV bitline differential tips it into oscillation whose starting phase encodes the bit, captured by a flip-flop in ~2 ns. Proven on an open 130 nm shuttle with on-chip bitline/cell-cap replicas for <$1M in 24 months.
why: Fact 1/7: gain near criticality (>40 dB at microamp bias) could halve the required bitline signal, enabling longer bitlines with fewer sense amps or smaller Cs.

title: Saprotroph recycling: retired DDR4 DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Saprotrophic fungi turn dead wood into new growth. An FPGA CXL Type-3 card hosts 8-16 salvaged DDR4 RDIMMs from retired servers and takes over the aged chips' 'periphery intelligence': per-DIMM retention profiling, chipkill ECC, adaptive refresh and bad-row remap, so they serve as a slower tier. One board spin plus firmware, ~$800k in 24 months, with revenue from refurbished pools.
why: Supply axis: hyperscalers retire millions of DDR4 DIMMs. Reusing even 10% adds memory at ~10-20% of new DDR5 cost/bit with zero fab capex.

title: Lizard-tail autotomy: salvaging fab-reject dies by amputating failed mats
idea: Lizards shed a tail to survive. Buy DRAM dies that fail final test on a few unrepairable mats or a dead sense-amp stripe, map those regions out with post-package repair plus a controller remap table, and sell them as odd-capacity modules (e.g., 14 GB) for caching tiers. $1M covers a used-tester test flow and first lots within 24 months.
why: Supply axis: turns several % of yield fallout into sellable bits at a fraction of new cost/bit, with no fab capex.

title: Otoacoustic diagnostics: supply-current spectra reveal DRAM sense margin
idea: Healthy cochleae emit faint sounds that allow non-invasive hearing tests. Standard activate/read bursts run while a fast shunt samples DIMM supply current. The spectral shape of sense-amp and restore transients exposes weak banks, timing margin and aging without vendor test modes. A $20k scope plus an ML classifier trained on 1,000 DIMMs, ~$400k in 18 months.
why: Supply axis: grades used and salvaged DRAM in seconds instead of hours of pattern testing, and sets per-DIMM refresh/timing.

title: Gecko-setae microfiber probe card contacting every die at once
idea: Gecko feet make reliable contact through millions of compliant setae. A probe card made of conductive CNT-cored polymer micro-pillars, molded from a reusable silicon master, touches every die on a 300 mm wafer at once with gentle self-conforming force. On-die BIST means each die needs only power plus a serial line. University-cleanroom molding and prototype, ~$900k in 24 months.
why: Capital/test: one touchdown per wafer with cheap replicated cards could cut test cost per bit 30-50% and free tester capex.

title: Cuckoo strategy: host raises the on-die ECC and hammer logic
idea: Cuckoos let other birds raise their chicks. Write a JEDEC-style proposal plus open reference RTL in which the host controller does what each die's periphery does today (on-die ECC, refresh-management counters, thermal refresh) using metadata in ordinary rows, so 'lean' dies can omit those circuits. Three engineers, FPGA demo and standards work, ~$900k in 24 months.
why: Fact 7: on-die ECC alone adds ~6% array plus logic. Moving it and hammer counters to the host could reclaim ~6-10% die area per bit.

title: Moth-ear minimal-periphery eDRAM compiler for open U.S. PDKs
idea: Noctuid moths detect bats with ears of just two neurons. An open-source compiler for SkyWater 130/GF180 generates 3T gain-cell eDRAM macros with radically minimal periphery: single-ended inverter sensing, shared counter refresh and standard-cell decoders. Two shuttles validate it for ~$700k in 24 months.
why: U.S. manufacturability: gives domestic mature-node fabs a working-memory macro ~2-3x denser than SRAM for chiplets now, seeding a U.S. DRAM design base.

title: Termite-mound chimney DIMM shroud enabling refresh downshift
idea: Termite mounds hold steady temperatures with passive convection chimneys. 3D-printed DIMM shrouds with mound-like chimney and tunnel geometry use existing server airflow to keep DRAM under ~45 C. A BIOS policy, keyed to the on-DIMM temperature sensor, leaves 2x refresh mode and stretches refresh when the sensor confirms cool operation. CFD plus prototypes, ~$300k in 12 months.
why: Fact 3: retention roughly doubles per ~10 C. Running ~15 C cooler avoids 2x refresh and cuts refresh energy and bandwidth loss ~50%.

title: Bat-echolocation TDR to find and remap marginal HBM TSVs
idea: Bats map their world from echo delays. Picosecond time-domain reflectometry through HBM test and boundary-scan paths measures impedance discontinuities in each TSV/microbump lane, flags marginal (resistive or voided) ones before they fail, and remaps them to HBM's existing spare lanes. Instrument plus algorithm work on stack samples, ~$800k in 24 months.
why: Fact 6: TSV/bump defects drive much of the 20-30% stack yield loss. Earlier, finer detection with remap could recover several points of yield and cut HBM cost/bit.

title: Predictive-coding memory link transmitting only prediction errors
idea: The visual cortex sends mostly prediction errors, not raw images. Identical lightweight predictors (last-value, stride, zero-run) sit at both ends of a CXL/DIMM link on FPGA, and only the entropy-coded XOR residual crosses the wire. FPGA prototype, ~$600k in 18 months.
why: Fact 5: residuals are mostly zeros, so ~1.5-2x fewer bits cross a 10-20 pJ/bit link. That buys effective bandwidth and energy and lets fewer channels feed the same compute.

title: CRISPR spacer library of row-hammer attack signatures
idea: Bacteria keep snippets of past viral DNA as spacers to recognize reinfection. The controller keeps a compact CAM of hashed aggressor-pattern signatures (address deltas, cadence relative to refresh), shared fleet-wide by firmware update, and triggers targeted refresh only on matches, over a cheap probabilistic baseline. Firmware, FPGA and attack corpus, ~$500k in 18 months.
why: Fact 9: learns new many-sided patterns after first sighting while issuing ~5x fewer mitigation refreshes than blanket probabilistic schemes.

title: Cicada prime-period refresh jitter defeating hammer synchronization
idea: Periodical cicadas emerge on prime cycles (13, 17 years) so predators cannot sync with them. Controller firmware schedules REF commands per bank at co-prime, jittered intervals within DDR5's postpone/pull-in allowance (mean stays tREFI). Neither workloads nor attackers can then phase-lock activations to in-DRAM TRR sampling windows. Firmware plus FPGA tests, ~$250k in 12 months.
why: Fact 9: synchronization-based patterns defeat TRR. Desynchronizing restores TRR effectiveness with zero die area.

title: Mayfly memory: refresh-free banks for data that dies young
idea: Adult mayflies live a day and have no working gut, so no maintenance organs for a short life. An allocator flag marks 'ephemeral' pages (AI activations, KV scratch, network buffers) that are rewritten within the 64 ms guaranteed retention. The controller skips refresh, or uses partial-array refresh, for banks holding only such data. Linux patch, controller firmware and FPGA demo, ~$600k in 24 months.
why: Fact 3: recovers the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and refresh energy on the large share of AI memory that is short-lived.

title: Henneman size-principle recruitment of charge-pump units
idea: Muscles recruit small motor units first and large ones only under heavy load (Henneman's size principle). Each VPP/VBB pump is split into binary-weighted units (1x, 2x, 4x, 8x) enabled in order by a load monitor, so light loads run on small units at peak efficiency. Validated on a 65/130 nm MPW test chip and licensed, ~$700k in 24 months.
why: Fact 10/idle power: pumps are 20-40% efficient at light load. Recruitment roughly doubles that, cutting VPP/VBB standby and refresh power ~30-50%.

title: Elephantnose-fish impedance spectroscopy fixture catching counterfeit DRAM
idea: Elephantnose fish identify objects by how they distort a self-made electric field. A low-cost fixture sweeps tiny AC signals (10 kHz-1 GHz) across each DRAM package's pins and matches the impedance spectrum to genuine-die references, flagging remarked, recycled or wrong-die parts in seconds. VNA-based fixture plus reference database, ~$350k in 12 months.
why: Supply axis: in a 4x price spike, grey-market fakes surge. Trusted screening lets OEMs safely tap secondary supply.

title: Dolphin unihemispheric sleep: mirrored hot pages across alternately refreshing subchannels
idea: Dolphins sleep one brain hemisphere at a time. The controller mirrors only the hottest ~1-2% of pages across the two DDR5 subchannels, refreshes them in alternation and steers reads to the awake copy, so refresh never stalls hot reads. Controller RTL plus FPGA evaluation, ~$400k in 18 months.
why: Fact 3: hides the refresh stalls behind the 10-20% bandwidth loss for latency-critical hot data, at a ~1-2% capacity cost.
